idiom_name: HashMap<Long, Memo> + getOrPut with a non-null sealed Memo
implementation_notes: The Kotlin stdlib reduces the memo idiom to one call - mutableMapOf plus getOrPut(key) { compute() } - so each rule reads as a single expression, and the memo value must be a non-null sealed type (Memo.Ok(node, next) / Memo.Fail) because getOrPut treats a stored null as a missing value and would recompute the rule on every hit; the stdlib points to getOrPutIfNull/getOrPutIfMissing for maps that may hold nulls. What replaces the classic memo-table object is that the table is a private HashMap<Long, Memo> field with a packed (ruleId shl 32) or pos key while the rules stay ordinary member functions. If the memo is a ConcurrentHashMap, note the documented caveat that getOrPut may still invoke the default function when the key is present, so the memoized computation must be side-effect free.
pitfalls: getOrPut re-evaluates whenever the key is absent or mapped to null, so a nullable memo value silently disables memoization - store a non-null Fail object instead.
On a ConcurrentMap, getOrPut documents that the default function may run even when the key is present: the rule body must be pure if the memo is shared.
HashMap<Long, ...> boxes the key on every lookup; a packed Int key where positions are bounded, or a HashMap<Pair<Int, Int>, Memo>, trades allocation for readability.
